blocks.text: After a knife wound to the back, a man can feel a pin-prick on his left leg but cannot feel a vibrating tuning fork on it, while his right leg is the opposite: he feels the vibration but not the pin. The two sides of the body are reporting different senses, which only makes sense if different sensory pathways cross at different levels.

blocks.markdown: **Somatosensation** is the sensation of touch, pressure, vibration, proprioception, temperature and pain from the body. Each begins with a **primary afferent** whose cell body lies in a **dorsal root ganglion** (or a cranial ganglion for the head). The afferent carries information in one of two main ascending pathways. Receptors are classified by **modality** (what they detect), **adaptation** (how they behave during a constant stimulus) and **fibre type**.

rows: Sustained pressure, fine spatial detail, edges
blocks.caption: A rapidly adapting receptor signals change; a slowly adapting one signals the maintained stimulus.

blocks.title: Classifying a receptor from its behaviour
blocks.prompt: A feather is brushed lightly across the fingertip. The afferent fires in a brief burst and then falls silent even though the feather stays in contact. Which receptor type is most likely involved, and why?

steps.text: The afferent fires only at the onset, so it adapts rapidly and signals change rather than maintained contact.
The stimulus is light touch on glabrous skin, which points to a superficial receptor.
Meissner corpuscles are superficial, rapidly adapting low-threshold touch receptors.

blocks.answer: A Meissner corpuscle. A slowly adapting Merkel cell afferent would continue firing under maintained contact.

blocks.markdown:
**The dorsal column-medial lemniscal (DC-ML) pathway** carries discriminative touch, vibration and conscious proprioception. The primary afferent enters the cord and ascends **ipsilaterally** in the **dorsal columns** (fasciculus gracilis for the lower body, fasciculus cuneatus for the upper). It synapses in the **nucleus gracilis or cuneatus** in the caudal medulla; second-order fibres **decussate in the medulla** (internal arcuate fibres), form the **medial lemniscus**, and relay in the **ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus** of the thalamus before reaching the primary somatosensory cortex.

**The spinothalamic (anterolateral) pathway** carries pain, temperature and crude touch. The primary afferent synapses in the **dorsal horn** within one or two segments of entry; second-order fibres **decussate in the anterior white commissure** within a few segments and ascend **contralaterally** in the anterolateral white matter to the VPL thalamus and then the cortex.

rows: In the cord, anterior white commissure, 1-2 segments of entry

blocks.title: Dissociated sensory loss
blocks.text: Because the two pathways cross at different levels, a lesion in the cord can remove one modality and spare the other. Pain and temperature loss with preserved vibration and proprioception, or the reverse, is called dissociated sensory loss and localises the lesion by showing which tract is affected.

blocks.title: Left hemisection of the cord at T10
blocks.prompt: A knife injury cuts the left half of the spinal cord at T10 (Brown-Sequard pattern). Predict the sensory findings below the lesion.

steps.text: The left dorsal column carries ipsilateral vibration and proprioception, so these are lost on the left below T10.

Spinothalamic fibres from the right leg enter on the right, cross near their level of entry (below the lesion), and then ascend on the left. They therefore pass through the cut left half of the cord and are interrupted. Fibres from the left leg crossed to the right below the lesion and ascend in the intact right half.
Thus pain and temperature are lost on the right below the lesion, beginning one or two segments below it. Light touch is often preserved on both sides because it travels in both pathways.

blocks.answer: Left: loss of vibration and proprioception (with ipsilateral upper motor neurone weakness). Right: loss of pain and temperature a segment or two below T10.

items: Posterior (dorsal column) disease, such as B12 deficiency or neurosyphilis, impairs vibration and position sense with relatively preserved pain and temperature.

Central cord lesions (a cavity or syrinx) interrupt crossing spinothalamic fibres in the anterior white commissure, giving bilateral segmental loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch and proprioception.
Cortical representation (the sensory homunculus) lies in the postcentral gyrus, with the leg medial and the face and hand lateral.

blocks.title: Do not decide laterality from the symptom alone
blocks.text: Dorsal column signs are ipsilateral to a cord lesion, but spinothalamic signs are contralateral. Always ask which tract carries the modality before choosing a side.

points: Cutaneous receptors are classified by modality and adaptation: Meissner and Pacinian are rapidly adapting, Merkel and Ruffini slowly adapting, free endings detect pain and temperature.
The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carries touch, vibration and proprioception, ascends ipsilaterally and decussates in the medulla.
The spinothalamic tract carries pain, temperature and crude touch and decussates in the cord within a few segments of entry.
Dissociated sensory loss and its laterality localise a cord lesion.

questions.stem: Which cutaneous receptor is most sensitive to high-frequency vibration, such as that from a 128 Hz tuning fork placed on a bony prominence?

distractorRationale.a: Merkel complexes are slowly adapting and detect sustained pressure and form.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting and tuned to vibration.
distractorRationale.c: Free endings mainly detect pain and temperature.

questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are deep, rapidly adapting receptors with a lamellar capsule that filters out slow changes, making them best at detecting vibration. Vibration is tested clinically with a tuning fork.

questions.stem: A receptor fires continuously for as long as a small object presses on the skin, and gives high-resolution information about the object's edges. Which receptor is this?

distractorRationale.b: Meissner corpuscles adapt rapidly and signal motion across the skin.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: Merkel cell complexes adapt slowly and give fine spatial detail.
distractorRationale.d: A muscle spindle is a proprioceptor, not a cutaneous receptor.

questions.explanation: Sustained firing indicates slow adaptation, and fine edge detail indicates a small receptive field and superficial location. These are the properties of Merkel cell complexes.

questions.stem: Which receptor type principally detects painful and thermal stimuli in the skin?

options.text: Free nerve endings of thin myelinated and unmyelinated fibres

questions.correctOptionText: Free nerve endings of thin myelinated and unmyelinated fibres

distractorRationale.a: Correct: A-delta and C fibre free endings carry nociceptive and thermal signals.
distractorRationale.d: Golgi tendon organs sense muscle tension.

questions.explanation: Nociceptors and thermoreceptors are free nerve endings of thinly myelinated A-delta fibres and unmyelinated C fibres. Encapsulated receptors such as Pacinian and Meissner corpuscles detect mechanical stimuli.

questions.stem: Fine touch and conscious proprioception from the left foot travel in the dorsal column on the left side of the cord. At what level does the second-order neurone of this pathway cross the midline?

options.text: In the spinal cord, within one or two segments of entry
In the caudal medulla, after synapsing in the nucleus gracilis

questions.correctOptionText: In the caudal medulla, after synapsing in the nucleus gracilis

distractorRationale.a: That is the level of crossing of the spinothalamic tract.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: second-order fibres cross as internal arcuate fibres and form the medial lemniscus.
distractorRationale.c: The thalamus is the relay to the cortex, not the site of crossing.
distractorRationale.d: The internal capsule carries fibres already crossed.

questions.explanation: Dorsal column afferents ascend uncrossed to the nucleus gracilis (lower limb) or cuneatus (upper limb). Their second-order fibres decussate in the caudal medulla as the internal arcuate fibres.

questions.stem: Where do the second-order neurones of the spinothalamic pathway cross the midline?

options.text: In the anterior white commissure of the cord, within a few segments of entry

questions.correctOptionText: In the anterior white commissure of the cord, within a few segments of entry

distractorRationale.a: Medullary crossing is for the dorsal column pathway.
distractorRationale.b: No major sensory decussation occurs in the pons for this pathway.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: spinothalamic second-order fibres cross near their level of entry.
distractorRationale.d: They do cross, which is why pain and temperature loss is contralateral.

questions.explanation: Spinothalamic second-order neurones in the dorsal horn cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the contralateral anterolateral column. This early crossing explains contralateral pain and temperature loss after a cord hemisection.

questions.stem: True or false: pain and temperature fibres ascend in the dorsal columns on the same side as the stimulus.
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic tract, which crosses within the cord and ascends contralaterally. The dorsal columns carry ipsilateral fine touch, vibration and proprioception.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with vitamin B12 deficiency has unsteady gait worse in the dark, with loss of vibration and joint position sense in both feet. Pain and temperature sensation is normal. Which part of the cord is predominantly affected?

distractorRationale.a: Spinothalamic damage would impair pain and temperature, which are normal.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: vibration and proprioception loss with preserved pain and temperature indicates dorsal column dysfunction.
distractorRationale.c: Anterior horn damage causes lower motor neurone weakness.
distractorRationale.d: Anterior commissure damage affects crossing pain and temperature fibres.

questions.explanation: Loss of vibration and joint position sense with preserved pain and temperature is dissociated sensory loss pointing to the dorsal columns. Worsening in the dark reflects reliance on proprioception when vision cannot compensate.

questions.stem: A patient has loss of vibration and joint position sense in the right leg and loss of pin-prick and temperature sensation in the left leg and trunk, beginning a few segments below the umbilicus. Which lesion best explains this?

options.text: Left hemisection of the cord at the lower thoracic level
Right hemisection of the lower thoracic cord
Central cavity in the cervical cord
Lesion of the left medial lemniscus in the pons

questions.correctOptionText: Right hemisection of the lower thoracic cord

distractorRationale.a: A left hemisection gives left dorsal column loss and right spinothalamic loss, the opposite of this pattern.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: right dorsal column loss (ipsilateral) with left pain and temperature loss (contralateral) fits a right hemicord lesion.
distractorRationale.c: A cervical central lesion would affect arms and be bilateral.
distractorRationale.d: A medial lemniscus lesion would give contralateral loss of all dorsal-column modalities.

questions.explanation: Dorsal column modalities are lost on the same side as a hemicord lesion, whereas spinothalamic modalities are lost on the opposite side. Right dorsal column loss with left pain and temperature loss therefore indicates a right hemisection at the lower thoracic level.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a cavity (syrinx) in the centre of her cervical spinal cord. She has lost pain and temperature in both arms in a shawl distribution but feels light touch and vibration normally. Explain the anatomical basis.
markingGuide: Pain and temperature fibres synapse in the dorsal horn and cross in the anterior white commissure
The central cavity interrupts crossing fibres at those segments, on both sides
Loss is therefore bilateral and segmental (arms and upper trunk)
Dorsal columns lie posteriorly and are spared, preserving vibration and proprioception
Light touch is preserved because it is also carried by dorsal columns
questions.explanation: A central syrinx destroys the anterior white commissure where second-order spinothalamic fibres cross, so pain and temperature are lost at those segments on both sides. The dorsal columns are outside the lesion, so touch and vibration are preserved.

questions.stem: Contrast the dorsal column-medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways in terms of modalities, site of first synapse, level of decussation and side of ascent relative to the stimulus.
markingGuide: DC-ML: fine touch, vibration, conscious proprioception; spinothalamic: pain, temperature, crude touch
DC-ML first synapse in nucleus gracilis/cuneatus of the medulla; spinothalamic in dorsal horn
DC-ML decussates in the medulla; spinothalamic in the cord (anterior white commissure) within a few segments of entry
DC-ML ascends ipsilaterally in the cord; spinothalamic contralaterally
Both relay in the VPL nucleus of the thalamus to the primary somatosensory cortex
questions.explanation: The two pathways differ in what they carry and where they cross, which is why a cord lesion can dissociate modalities. Both converge on the VPL thalamus and the postcentral gyrus.
